headline.en: A Hidden Crack Was Found in the Code Behind Most Websites

hook.en: Computer experts found a dangerous weak spot in PHP, a kind of code that runs most of the world's websites. Hackers who found the weak spot first could have taken control of those websites. So big tech companies and even the FBI raced to fix it before anyone could use it to cause harm.

en: Imagine almost every website you visit is built like a house. PHP is one of the main kinds of wood used to build those houses. Experts think about 7 out of every 10 websites use it somewhere.

Recently, computer researchers found a crack in that wood. It was a flaw so serious that if hackers found it first, they could sneak in and take over a website's computer completely, like finding a secret unlocked door into someone's house.

This crack was found partly with help from AI tools, the same kind of smart computer programs that can write essays or answer questions. The FBI, which is part of the American government that handles crime, sent out an urgent warning telling companies to fix their systems immediately, or shut them down if they could not fix them fast enough.

Huge companies like Amazon, Google, and OpenAI fixed their own systems within hours. So far, no one has publicly reported a successful break-in using this crack. This story is about a race: fixing the crack before any hacker can use it, not about an attack that already happened.

why_it_matters.en: Websites you use every day, like games, school tools, or video sites, might run on PHP without you ever knowing it. When experts fix a crack like this fast, it is part of why the internet usually stays safe for you to use.

def.en: A type of computer code that tells websites what to do, used by most websites on the internet.
A fix that computer experts add to code to close up a dangerous crack or weakness.

question.en: Should companies have to tell everyone right away when they find a dangerous crack like this, even before it is fixed?

en: People deserve to know if their information might be at risk.
Telling everyone fast means more experts can help find a fix.
Keeping it secret could mean some hackers already know and are using it quietly.

label.en: No, fix it first, then tell people

en: Announcing the crack before it is fixed is like shouting the location of an unlocked door to everyone, including hackers.
A quiet, careful fix can happen faster without a public panic.
Some companies need time to test a fix properly before announcing it, or the fix itself could cause new problems.

question.en: Is it a good idea that AI tools helped find this dangerous crack in the first place?

label.en: Yes, finding it with AI was a good thing

en: Finding the crack early meant good guys could fix it before most hackers noticed.
AI can search through huge amounts of code faster than people alone ever could.
Using AI for safety checks could help find other hidden problems before they cause harm.

label.en: No, it shows a worrying new danger

en: If AI can find these cracks for good guys, it can also find them for hackers, maybe even faster.
This shows that future hacking attacks might happen at a speed humans cannot keep up with.
Relying on AI to find flaws might make people less careful about writing safe code in the first place.

headline.en: A Hole Found in the Code That Runs Most of the Internet — and a Race to Patch It Before Hackers Do

hook.en: On October 21, 2026, security researchers revealed a serious flaw in PHP, the programming language that quietly powers an estimated seven out of ten websites on Earth. The bug, nicknamed 'PHP2Shell' in news coverage, could let an attacker seize control of an affected server. The FBI told organisations to patch immediately or take vulnerable systems offline, and companies including Amazon, Google and OpenAI scrambled to fix their own systems within hours.

en: Most people have never heard of PHP, but almost everyone has used something built with it. It is a programming language written in the 1990s that handles the behind-the-scenes work of websites — pulling your order history on a shopping site, checking your password when you log in, deciding what to show you on a news feed. It runs quietly under huge chunks of the web, including many government, business and media sites, which is why a serious flaw in it is not a niche problem but a structural one.

The flaw discovered this week was severe because of what it allowed: an attacker who found the right weak spot could potentially run their own commands on someone else's server, essentially taking over a machine that was never supposed to be theirs to control. Researchers reportedly used AI tools to help find the exact weakness, which is itself part of the story — the same kind of artificial intelligence that can write an email can now help both defenders and attackers comb through code looking for cracks, and it can do it far faster than a human alone.

That speed is why the response was so urgent. The FBI's Cyber Division — the branch of the agency that deals with digital crime rather than physical crime — issued an advisory telling organisations to 'immediately update affected PHP installations,' and said that if a fix wasn't ready yet, the safer move was to disconnect the vulnerable system entirely rather than leave it exposed. That is an unusually blunt instruction; agencies don't often tell businesses to simply switch things off.

Big technology companies did not wait around. Amazon, Google and OpenAI reportedly patched their own affected systems within hours of the flaw becoming public, which is fast by the standards of large organisations, where updates normally go through layers of testing before anything changes. The hurry reflects a new worry in cybersecurity: if AI can help attackers find and exploit a weakness automatically, the window between 'the flaw is public' and 'someone is already using it' might shrink from weeks to hours.

As of this reporting, no confirmed large-scale break-ins tied to the flaw had been made public. That matters, because it means this is a story about prevention, not disaster — the race to lock the door before anyone tries the handle, rather than a report of a robbery that already happened. Whether that race was won will become clear over the coming weeks, as security researchers watch for signs that the flaw was used against targets who were too slow to patch.

why_it_matters.en: Even if you've never written a line of code, the websites you use every day — for school, shopping, banking, games — very likely rely on PHP somewhere in the background, which is why a flaw like this is less like a crack in one house and more like a crack in the foundation material used across an entire neighbourhood. It's also an early, concrete example of AI changing the pace of cybersecurity itself, for both the people trying to break in and the people trying to keep them out.

def.en: A programming language, first released in the 1990s, that handles much of the behind-the-scenes work on a large share of the world's websites.
A weakness in a piece of software that could let someone do something they shouldn't, such as take control of a system.
An update released to fix a specific problem in software, especially a security weakness.

question.en: Should AI tools capable of finding security flaws in software be developed and shared openly, or kept tightly restricted?

en: Open access lets defenders everywhere, not just large companies, find and fix flaws in their own systems before attackers do.
Restricting the technology mainly slows down responsible researchers, since well-funded attackers can likely build or acquire similar tools anyway.
Historically, openly published vulnerability research has made software safer over time by forcing fixes faster.
A tool that finds flaws works exactly as well for an attacker planning a break-in as for a defender trying to prevent one.
Wide distribution means less time to quietly fix a problem before it becomes public knowledge that criminals can act on immediately.
Governments and large firms can patch fast; smaller organisations and individuals often cannot, so broad disclosure helps the strong and hurts the weak.

question.en: Should companies be legally required to patch critical security flaws within a strict deadline, such as 24 hours?

en: A hard deadline forces organisations to treat security as urgent rather than something to schedule around other priorities.
When a flaw is this widespread, slow patching by even a few major systems creates risk for everyone connected to them.
Clear legal rules give security teams inside a company the authority to demand resources and attention immediately, rather than waiting for approval.
Rushed patches, applied without proper testing, can break other parts of a system and sometimes cause more damage than the original flaw.
Organisations vary hugely in size and complexity, and a deadline that works for a small website may be unrealistic for a hospital's medical records system.
Flexibility lets organisations prioritise based on their actual exposure and risk, rather than following a one-size-fits-all rule that ignores their specific situation.

headline.en: Tech Company Stock Prices Take a Wild Rollercoaster Ride

hook.en: This week, the prices of many big technology companies' stocks jumped up and then crashed down. People who own tiny pieces of these companies are nervous about one thing: the huge amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence, or AI. Even companies that made more money than expected still saw their stock prices fall hard.

en: Imagine a company is like a big pizza. You can buy a tiny slice of that pizza, called a share. If people think the pizza company will grow and make more pizzas, your slice becomes worth more money. If people get worried, your slice can be worth less, even quickly.

This week, slices of big tech companies went on a rollercoaster. One day, stock markets jumped up. The very next day, they dropped hard. Companies that make computer chips for AI, like Nvidia and AMD, lost a lot of value. Even Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, saw its stock fall 8% in a single day, even though it had actually made more money than people expected.

Why would a successful company's slices get cheaper? Because AI needs enormous data centers; giant buildings packed with powerful computers that use huge amounts of electricity. Building and running these centers costs an incredible amount of money, like buying thousands of expensive video game consoles and leaving them running all day and night.

The boss of Nvidia, a man named Jensen Huang, said there isn't enough money available for everyone who wants to build these AI computer centers. That worried investors. They started wondering if companies are spending money faster than they can make it back, kind of like spending your whole piggy bank on toys before you know if you'll actually like them.

why_it_matters.en: Lots of families have money saved for the future in things connected to the stock market, like retirement accounts, even if they don't realize it. When tech stocks swing wildly, it can affect how much money is in those accounts. It also affects which new technologies get built, since companies need money to keep inventing things you might use someday.

def.en: A share is a tiny piece of a company that people can buy, hoping it becomes worth more money over time.
A data center is a huge building full of powerful computers that run things like AI programs, and it uses enormous amounts of electricity.

question.en: Is it a good idea for companies to spend enormous amounts of money on AI before they're sure it will pay off?

en: Big risks can lead to big rewards, like planting seeds now for a harvest later.
Companies that invest early in new technology often become the leaders everyone else follows.
Waiting too long to try something new could mean falling behind forever.
Spending that much money without knowing it will work could put companies in serious trouble.
If the AI investment fails, many workers could lose their jobs.
Spending so much on AI takes money away from other things the company could do right now.

question.en: Should people worry about a company's stock falling even when the company is actually doing well right now?

en: Investors care about what might happen in the future, not just how things look today.
If spending gets out of control, today's success might not last very long.
It's smart to ask hard questions before small problems turn into big ones.
The company is still making more money than people expected, which is good news.
Stock markets often swing up and down because of feelings, not because of real problems.
Panicking and selling stocks can unfairly hurt companies that are actually doing just fine.

headline.en: The AI Boom Hits a Nervous Patch on Wall Street

hook.en: US stock markets lurched up and then down this week as investors got cold feet about the staggering cost of building artificial intelligence. The Nasdaq Composite, a stock index that tracks mostly tech companies, fell 2.9% on Thursday after a strong rally the day before, and even a company with excellent results, Meta Platforms, saw its shares drop 8%. The worry wasn't bad news about any single company — it was a sudden question hanging over the whole industry: can anyone actually afford all this?

en: On Wednesday, strong earnings from companies linked to SpaceX and Tesla sent stocks climbing. By Thursday the mood had flipped entirely. The Nasdaq Composite — an index, or running scoreboard, that adds up the share prices of thousands of companies, heavily weighted toward tech — dropped 2.9% in a single day. The broader S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the largest US companies across every industry, fell 1.4%. These are large one-day moves for indexes that normally shift by fractions of a percent.

The strangest part of the day was Meta Platforms, the company behind Facebook and Instagram. Meta's results actually beat what Wall Street analysts had expected, and the company even gave upbeat guidance — its own forecast of how well it expects to perform in the months ahead. Normally that would send a stock up. Instead, Meta's shares fell 8%. Investors weren't doubting Meta's current business; they were worried about how much money Meta and its rivals are pouring into AI, and whether that spending will ever pay for itself.

Chipmakers took an even harder hit. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 8%, Micron Technology dropped 6%, and Nvidia — the company whose chips power most of the world's AI systems — fell 4%. These companies make the hardware inside data centers, the huge warehouses full of computers that train and run AI programs. If investors think the AI buildout might slow down, the companies selling the shovels get hit even before the companies doing the digging. Shares in power and energy firms that supply electricity to data centers also fell, since those businesses only make sense if the data centers keep expanding.

Nvidia's own chief executive, Jensen Huang, put his finger on the underlying fear. 'There's a scarcity of capital,' he said — capital meaning the pool of money that banks, investors, and companies have available to lend or spend. 'The demand [for] the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital.' In plain terms: the amount of money companies want to spend building AI infrastructure is growing faster than the amount of money the financial system can comfortably supply, which raises the cost of borrowing and the risk that some bets won't pay off.

What makes this moment different from a normal bad day in the market is what it isn't about. Nobody is saying AI doesn't work, or that these companies are badly run. The question investors are suddenly asking out loud is whether the entire industry is spending money faster than it can be justified by what AI actually earns back — a reassessment of the whole boom, not a verdict on any one company's quarter.

why_it_matters.en: If you or your parents have money in a pension, a retirement account, or an index fund, there's a good chance a slice of it is tied up in exactly these companies, since AI-related stocks have been one of the biggest drivers of the entire stock market's growth. A sustained slowdown in AI spending wouldn't just hit tech workers — it could ripple into electricity prices, construction jobs building data centers, and the pace at which AI tools show up in schools, hospitals, and everyday apps.

def.en: A number that adds up the share prices of many companies to show, at a glance, whether a market or industry is rising or falling overall.
Money that a business can raise or borrow to invest in things like equipment, buildings, or growth.
A large building full of powerful computers that store information and run programs, including the ones that power AI.

question.en: Is the huge amount of money being poured into AI a smart long-term investment or a bubble that's bound to burst?

en: Every major technology shift — railroads, electricity, the internet — required massive upfront spending before it paid off, and AI is unlikely to be different.
Companies like Meta and Nvidia are still profitable and growing, which suggests the spending is backed by real revenue, not just hope.
Falling behind on AI infrastructure now could mean permanently losing ground to competitors or other countries that keep building.
When even strong earnings and good forecasts can't stop a stock from falling, it suggests prices were inflated by hype rather than realistic expectations.
A CEO publicly admitting that demand for money outstrips the supply of money is a warning sign markets have seen before previous crashes.
Pouring money into data centers and chips before it's clear how AI will reliably make a profit risks stranding billions of dollars in assets nobody ends up needing.

question.en: When investors get nervous, should companies keep spending aggressively on AI or pull back to reassure the market?

en: Slowing down now could hand a permanent advantage to rivals who keep building through the uncertainty.
Stock prices swing for all sorts of reasons, and basing long-term strategy on short-term market mood can be a mistake.
The companies spending the most, like Meta, are still generating strong revenue, suggesting they can afford to keep investing even if their stock dips.
Spending money the financial system can't comfortably supply, as Nvidia's own CEO warned, risks a harder financial reckoning later.
Markets are sending a clear signal that investors doubt the current pace is sustainable, and ignoring that signal can be costly.
A more cautious pace lets companies prove AI's profitability step by step, rather than betting enormous sums on an unproven timeline.

headline.en: Supreme Court Says: Don't Stop This Medical Care in Prisons Yet

hook.en: On Wednesday, the United States Supreme Court made a decision about transgender people in federal prisons. Transgender people are people whose gender does not match the sex they were given at birth. The Court said the government must keep giving them certain medical care while a bigger court case about it keeps going.

en: The government, led by President Trump, wanted to stop giving special medical care to transgender people locked up in federal prisons. This care helps their bodies match their gender.
A court case started over whether the government is allowed to stop it. That case is still being argued. It could take a long time to finish.
The Supreme Court is the highest court in the country. It did not decide who is right yet. It just said: keep the care going for now, until the case is settled.
This is called a 'pause' decision. It means nothing changes today, but the real argument about what's fair is still happening in courtrooms.

why_it_matters.en: This story is about how courts can press 'pause' on a big decision while they figure out what's fair, kind of like a referee stopping a game to check a replay before deciding the call. It also shows how government rules can change, and how people who disagree with a rule can ask a judge to look at it closely before it takes effect.

def.en: The most powerful court in the United States, which makes final decisions about what the law allows.
Medical treatment that helps a transgender person's body match the gender they feel they are.

question.en: Should the government have to keep doing something the old way while a court case about it is still being decided?

label.en: Yes, keep things the same for now

en: If the care stops and then the court says it was wrong to stop, people may already have been harmed.
Changing something suddenly in the middle of an argument can feel unfair to the people affected.
Waiting lets everyone hear both sides before anything is changed for real.

label.en: No, let the government act right away

en: The government was elected to make decisions, and waiting years for a court case can get in the way of that.
If the court case eventually agrees the government was right, then everyone had to wait for nothing.
Rules that stay in place by default can be hard to undo later, even if they turn out to be wrong.

question.en: Should prisons be required to give this specific medical care to transgender inmates?

en: Prisons already have to give inmates medical care for other serious health needs, so this could be seen as just another kind of care.
Some people think prisons should only provide the most basic, essential medical care and nothing more.
Some taxpayers feel they shouldn't have to pay for this kind of treatment through government budgets.
Some people believe this is a decision that elected lawmakers should make, not judges or prison officials.

headline.en: Supreme Court Blocks Trump Administration From Cutting Off Care to Transgender Federal Inmates — For Now

hook.en: On Wednesday, the US Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration must keep providing gender-affirming medical care to transgender people held in federal prisons while a lawsuit over the policy plays out in lower courts. The administration had been trying to end that care as part of a wider push to roll back federal recognition of transgender people. The ruling doesn't settle who's ultimately right — it just freezes things in place until the case is fully argued.

en: Federal prisons in the US have, for several years, provided hormone therapy and other medical treatment to transgender inmates who request it and whose doctors recommend it, under a policy adopted by the Bureau of Prisons, the federal agency that runs the prison system. Earlier this year, the Trump administration moved to end that policy, arguing it was not required to provide this kind of care. Transgender inmates and civil rights groups sued, saying cutting off ongoing treatment could cause serious medical harm.

A lower federal court agreed to pause the administration's change while the lawsuit continues, meaning the old policy — keep providing the care — stayed in effect. The administration asked the Supreme Court to lift that pause so it could stop the care immediately. On Wednesday, the Court said no. The care keeps flowing while the legal fight continues.

It's worth being precise about what this ruling actually is. The Supreme Court did not decide whether the administration's underlying policy is constitutional or lawful — that question is still being argued in lower courts and could take months or years to resolve, and might eventually come back to the Supreme Court for a final answer. What the justices did this week was issue an injunction, a court order that keeps things as they currently are, used specifically to prevent harm that couldn't be undone if a court later ruled the other way. If a transgender inmate's hormone therapy had been cut off and the courts later found the cutoff illegal, that interruption couldn't simply be reversed after the fact — which is the kind of situation these emergency orders exist for.

This case sits inside a bigger story. Since taking office, the Trump administration has issued a series of executive orders and policy changes aimed at removing federal recognition and support for transgender people — covering passports, the military, school sports, and now prison healthcare. Supporters of these changes argue the federal government shouldn't be in the business of funding or facilitating gender transition, especially using taxpayer money for people convicted of crimes. Opponents argue that courts have long required prisons to provide medically necessary care to the people they incarcerate, and that gender-affirming treatment for some transgender inmates falls into that category under existing medical guidelines.

The specific reasoning the justices gave, and how each of them voted, wasn't fully detailed in the news coverage available — these emergency rulings are sometimes issued with limited or no written explanation, unlike the Court's major decisions after full argument. What's clear is the practical result: the policy stands for now, the lawsuit keeps moving through lower courts, and this almost certainly isn't the last time this dispute reaches the Supreme Court.

why_it_matters.en: This case is a window into how the US legal system actually slows down sudden changes in government policy — courts can freeze a decision in place while they work out whether it's lawful, rather than letting either side win by acting fastest. It also shows that a win in court right now isn't the end of a legal fight; it's often just one stage in a case that could run for years.

def.en: Medical treatment, such as hormone therapy, given to help a person's body match their gender identity.
A court order that pauses an action or keeps a situation unchanged until a legal dispute about it is resolved.
The US federal agency responsible for running the country's federal prison system, as opposed to state or local jails.

question.en: Should the government be required to pay for gender-affirming medical care for transgender people in prison?

en: Courts have long held that prisons must give inmates medically necessary care, since people in custody can't get treatment on their own.
Suddenly stopping an ongoing hormone treatment can cause real physical and psychological harm that isn't easily reversed.
Major medical associations recognize this treatment as a legitimate part of care for some transgender patients, not an optional extra.
Taxpayers shouldn't be required to fund treatments that remain politically and medically contested for people convicted of crimes.
Prisons have limited budgets, and spending here means less for other medical needs across the inmate population.
Elected officials, not unelected prison administrators or judges, should decide what medical services the government is obligated to provide.

question.en: Should courts be able to freeze a government policy while a lawsuit against it is still being decided?

en: Some harms, like interrupting ongoing medical treatment, can't be undone later even if the courts eventually side against the policy.
Pausing preserves the situation fairly for both sides while the full legal process plays out, rather than letting one side's actions create facts on the ground.
The executive branch shouldn't be able to make sweeping, possibly illegal changes just because a final ruling will take years to arrive.
The elected administration was given authority to set policy, and courts pausing it before any final ruling blocks that authority without a clear legal finding of wrongdoing.
Long pauses can turn into years of the old policy staying in place by default, which itself has real costs and consequences.
Judges issuing these emergency orders often do so with little public explanation, which makes it hard to know whether the decision was well-reasoned.
